lines.raw: Here is a quick table.
lines.say: Here is a quick table.

lines.raw: Was the member covered? Date to use: Service date. Why: The service date must fall **inside** the coverage period. If Emily's insurance ended on 31 May, the June surgery would not be covered.
lines.say: Was the member covered? Date to use: Service date. Why: The service date must fall inside the coverage period. If Emily's insurance ended on 31 May, the June surgery would not be covered.

lines.raw: What care happened in March? Date to use: Service date. Why: Counts care by when it was given.
lines.say: What care happened in March? Date to use: Service date. Why: Counts care by when it was given.

lines.raw: How much money went out in March? Date to use: Paid date. Why: Counts money by when it left the insurer.
lines.say: How much money went out in March? Date to use: Paid date. Why: Counts money by when it left the insurer.

lines.raw: Was the claim sent on time? Date to use: Received date − service date. Why: Insurers set a **timely filing** deadline (often 90 days to 1 year). Late claims can be denied.
lines.say: Was the claim sent on time? Date to use: Received date − service date. Why: Insurers set a timely filing deadline (often 90 days to 1 year). Late claims can be denied.

lines.raw: How long was the stay? Date to use: Admission and discharge dates. Why: Length of stay.
lines.say: How long was the stay? Date to use: Admission and discharge dates. Why: Length of stay.

lines.raw: A report by service date and a report by paid date will never match exactly, and both are correct.

lines.raw: Claim lag and run-out.
lines.say: Claim lag and run-out.

lines.raw: Claims do not arrive the moment care happens.
lines.say: Claims do not arrive the moment care happens.

lines.raw: A provider may take days or weeks to send the bill, and the insurer then takes time to pay it.
lines.say: A provider may take days or weeks to send the bill, and the insurer then takes time to pay it.

lines.raw: This delay is called **claim lag**.
lines.say: This delay is called claim lag.

lines.raw: Claim lag.
lines.say: Claim lag.

lines.raw: Lag (days) equals Paid date − Service date.
lines.say: Lag (days) equals Paid date − Service date.

lines.raw: For example: Emily's hospital claim: 30 June − 2 June equals 28 days.
lines.say: For example: Emily's hospital claim: 30 June − 2 June equals 28 days.

lines.raw: Because of lag, the most recent months are always **incomplete**.
lines.say: Because of lag, the most recent months are always incomplete.

lines.raw: If you run a report on 1 July, many June visits have not been paid yet, so June looks cheaper than it really was.
lines.say: If you run a report on 1 July, many June visits have not been paid yet, so June looks cheaper than it really was.

lines.raw: The months of waiting for late claims to arrive are called the **run-out** period.
lines.say: The months of waiting for late claims to arrive are called the run-out period.

lines.raw: Analysts usually wait for a few months of **run-out** (often 3) before trusting a month's numbers, or they label the recent months as "incomplete".
